newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street puts sullen view on near-term outlook.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street puts sullen view on near-term outlook.

text.p: Wall Street enters the week with its near-term outlook a bit more sullen and stocks weighed down by a sharp bond market sell-off that for now has soured the interest rate environment.

Through November, stocks rolled higher without a hiccup, with the Dow industrials up a scorching 500 points for the month. The unbridled glee dimmed late last week when Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warned against "irrational exuberance" in the markets, spooking the market lower.

While the market's initial response to Greenspan's comments was sharp and negative -- the yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond completed a two-day surge back over 6.5 percent -- analysts doubted the market had been derailed.
"I think Greenspan is trying to talk the market down but I don't think this alters the course of the bull market," said Hildegard Zagorski, market analyst at Prudential Securities.
Whether or not recent events will prompt a change in the way investors view markets, there are signs that the frothiness that has accompanied the latest stage of the six-year run have abated.
For one, initial public offering activity has slowed dramatically from its peaks in April and May. A host of deals have been postponed in the last couple of weeks, a clear sign that demand has waned.

Also, some top Wall Street strategists have expressed heightened caution. One, Salomon Brothers chief equity strategist David Shulman, trimmed the percentage of stocks in two of his model asset allocation portfolios last week.

Several analysts said they thought Greenspan was hoping to accomplish with talk what he didn't dare do with monetary policy: a tempering of the increasing investor enthusiasm that had once again started to trickle down to secondary stocks.
While a monetary tightening would pull stock prices lower, it would also risk slowing an economy that is clearly having no trouble putting on the brakes without outside help.
On Friday, a very soft monthly jobs report showed payrolls grew at a surprisingly slow pace in November, diffusing concern about inflation.

"Inflation looks good and the numbers (Friday) were outright bullish for bonds," said Joseph Battipaglia, chief investment officer at Gruntal & Co. "There is a great deal of nervousness and people are looking for some sign that it's over, but it's not."

This week, markets will get their monthly double dose of inflation information, with the release of November's producer price index (PPI) Wednesday and the recently embattled consumer price index (CPI) Thursday.
Economists expect both indices to rise by 0.3 percentage points for the month. The core rates -- which exclude volatile food and energy prices -- are both forecast to rise by 0.2 percentage points.
Even with a rosy scenario in place, analysts said prices simply remain too high to warrant aggressive new purchases.

"I don't know why anyone would want to plunge in and buy at this point," said Allen Sinai, chief economist at Lehman Brothers Global Economic Advisors. "They might want to take profits on what was a good year."
